Rain significantly hampers optical flow estimation due to light interception, scattering, and shine. Conventional methods fall into two categories: either removing rain from images or computing indirect optical flow calculations under rain. These approaches have inherent limitations: rain elimination algorithms struggle with heavy rain and shine, while optical flow algorithms under rain often produce inaccurate results due to light interference. This research deviates from these two paths, instead using Disentangled Image Transformation (DIT) to simultaneously eliminate rain and estimate optical flow from undistorted images. DIT disentangles the transformations of rain effects and shine from those of background scenes, then computes flow from the underlying scenes. This method is mathematically sound and is experimentally proven to outperform state-of-the-art competitors on various metrics. DIT's design makes it easily integrable with deep learning architectures, and our code is available online for public use. DIT's flow estimates are accurate and shine-free, enabling post-processing treatments that further improve its performance. Comparative evaluations show that DIT-flow surpasses both rain-eliminated flow and indirect flow calculations on all metrics in heavily rain-afflicted and shine-containing images. DIT-flow also outperforms state-of-the-art flow algorithms, including medium-quality reference flow algorithms, in rain-free images. In contrast to removing rain from images or computing indirect flow calculations under rain, DIT resolves the light scattering issue by modeling the light transformation, rather than relying on image formation models. This leads to a more effective solution for computational resources. Notably, this method uses light modeling to compute flow from undistorted images, instead of deep learning-based rain removal algorithms that fail to deliver on heavy rain and shine challenges. This approach for deep learning-based rain elimination and optical flow estimation is now widely adopted in applications utilizing optical flow and image processing. However, some issues with shine remain in this work. Shine presents unique challenges to computer vision algorithms due to its brightness that can exceed the dynamic range of digital cameras, resulting in shaded areas with distorted colors, and reflected light that can interfere with optical flow estimation by illuminating some areas differently. While this work shows that deep learning-based models can compute optical flow from undistorted images free of light interference, shine-free optical flow algorithms are yet to be developed. Until such time, optical flow estimation under rain and shine remains an open research problem for computer vision. Reward learning via interactive feedback from humans is a promising approach for resolving sparsity issues with intrinsic motivation methods in reinforcement learning. However, relying on multiple feedback sources from a single human is not practical due to the high cost of giving feedback visually. Solving this problem, we develop a novel visually guided multi-cluster ranking task that can provide feedback for multiple states simultaneously. A key innovation in our research is the proposal of a cluster ranking model that can learn from limited visually-supplied reference feedback. Our results show that this model learns at a rate that is significantly faster than alternative methods, especially when data is limited. Our findings also reveal some valuable insights into the data requirements for ranking learning in complex scenarios. Our implementation and data are available online at https://github.com/AAUI-driving/visual-rl-sparse-rewards. Our research lays the ground for the development of low-cost human-in-the-loop methods that can efficiently learn rewards from human feedback in reinforcement learning. Our research is an extension of our previous work presented at the 2020 IJCAI conference. Our team won the 2020 Learning from Crowds Challenge at the 35th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) and achieved this success by solving the Visually Guided Multi-Cluster Ranking problem. Our achievement was recognized as the best performance among 24 participating teams. This talk concentrates on an intriguing connection between a famous cosmological theory called the Continuum Hypothesis and a specific class of mathematically consistent theories within Set Theory. The Continuum Hypothesis proposes to identify the number of real numbers within any given interval, essentially seeking to establish a clear, infinite quantity for this count. On the other hand, framework companionship, a concept born out of the Barwise-Kunen Chernoff theorem, allows us to analyze the scope or reach of a particular theory. When we consider two mathematically equivalent theories, we can leverage framework companionship to demonstrate that both theories share the same infinite proscriptions and consequently, the same parabolic structure. Notably, we can utilize this relationship to derive limitations on a dependent theory from its parent theory, and we explore several instances of this dependency with regard to set theoretical theories, ultimately focusing on the Continuum Hypothesis. We show that by applying framework companionship, we can derive a limit on the number of real numbers within any given interval as a countable union of smaller intervals, even in scenarios where the Hypothesis itself is abandoned. This leads to an interesting observation on the relationship between dependent set theoretical theories and their impact on the Continuum Hypothesis. Furthermore, we discuss multiple axiom systems, including those related to large cardinal axioms, and we explore how framework companionship can be employed to analyze the scope of these axiom systems, particularly in scenarios where the Continuum Hypothesis is unaffected. Additionally, we discuss numerous potential future research directions arising from our findings, especially in regards to the interplay between set theoretical models and the scope of true sentences within those models. This talk is an expansion of previous research presented in the 2019 North American meeting of the Association for Symbolic Logic and aims to provide a more comprehensive exploration of the relationship between framework companionship and the Continuum Hypothesis. Despite this constraint, there are specific linear systems where the HHL quantum algorithm achieves substantial speedups over classical methods. We explored the potential of combining HHL with classical numerical methods to solve a significant problem in financial risk management – the calculation of portfolio expectations. By linking HHL with classical Monte Carlo methods, we developed a hybrid approach that utilizes HHL to quickly obtain initial estimates and then updates the classical Monte Carlo method with this new information. Our results showed that this approach yields more accurate outcomes than classical Monte Carlo methods, especially in portfolios with highly correlated assets. Furthermore, the time complexity of this approach is comparable to that of classical Monte Carlo methods, making it an appealing solution for managing market risk in the current quantum computing era. To enhance data efficiency of end-to-end speech recognition, a multi-modal approach has been tested where text is incorporated during training. An initial method simply matched the speech and text distributions, but it didn't leverage the information effectively. Another approach involved conditioning the speech encoder on the text and using a text encoder that could be updated during training, but it introduced the challenge of maintaining a consistent text representation. Our proposed solution addresses these issues by utilizing a single text encoder that can learn the speech data during multi-modal training. Additionally, we introduced a bidirectional focus mechanism allowing the text and speech encoders to exchange information and allow the text to influence the speech encoder. This resulted in significant improvements in WER on the Librispeech dataset, achieving a particularly notable reduction in error rate for longer utterances. Our findings suggest that the proposed bidirectional focus mechanism can boost the performance of multi-modal speech recognition. Furthermore, our model performed on par with state-of-the-art single-modal models like Transley and MultiSpeech when the dataset is fully used. Nevertheless, when restricted to the same amount of speech data as the text dataset, multi-modal modeling still yielded a 6.3% WER improvement at the test set level. Our model also exhibited the capacity to generalize better than single-modal models, achieving a comparable performance to Transley when only 100 hours of data was utilized. Our implementation of the bidirectional focus mechanism resulted in a relatively modest increase in model parameters and a small additional computational cost. Nonetheless, our proposed approach offers the potential to generalize better than single-modal models at the some additional computational cost when only a limited amount of speech data is available. Our model also demonstrated the ability to detect utterances with no relevant text, thereby avoiding the learning of irrelevant text during multi-modal training. Our results showed that the proposed approach achieved a comparable WER to single-modal models on those utterances. Nonetheless, our method still faced the challenge of determining the optimal balance between single and multi-modal training. Our findings suggested that a balanced blend of single and multi-modal training yielded the best results, resulting in a 5.6% WER improvement at the test set level. A uniform parking function can be visualized as a sequence of intervals on the real line, where each interval represents the possible location for a car to park. The distribution of the starting point of these intervals, when they are evenly spaced, corresponds to a specific probability measure. This paper calculates key aspects of this distribution, including its mean, variance, moment ratios, and cumulative distribution function. Specifically, it shows that the mean of the starting point is the sum of the variances of the individual interval lengths, and that this measure is independent of the specific distribution of interval lengths. It also finds that the variance increases with the square of the number of intervals, and that this variance is directly proportional to the square of the sum of the squares of the individual interval lengths. Furthermore, it determines that the cumulative distribution function of the starting point can be compared to the distribution function of a specific quadratic expression. These calculations are valid for any number of intervals greater than one. This paper assumes a uniform distribution for the individual interval lengths, although the measures it calculates are independent of this specific distribution. It is reasonable to hypothesize that these results could be extended to other types of parking functions. The response to a drive current in the form of a pulse is variable and depends on the state of the system at the moment of measurement, indicating that the system is in a state of quantum entanglement with the measurement device. The duration of this entanglement can be altered by changing the drive current, which creates a bridge between two distinct equilibrium states and causes the system to exhibit jump phenomena due to a restriction in charge flow. This restriction is attributed to a blockage in the flow of a superflow component, rather than a result of the destruction of superconductivity. The duration of the jump can be altered by changing the strength of the magnetic field, which results in a greater than expected shift in the critical current. This phenomenon, in which the superflow component plays a crucial role, may have implications for the use of superconducting nanowires in sensing devices. The duration of the jump can also be altered by changing the properties of the nanowire, which suggests a possibility of controlling this phenomenon with an electric gate. Measurements of the critical current show that a critical point can be shifted by changing the drive current, the magnetic field, or the properties of the nanowire, which indicates a relationship between this point and the flow of a superflow component. However, this analysis does not take into account a phase shift that results from a drive current, which may change the phase of the system in a manner that affects the flow of the superflow component. The inclusion of this effect changes the interpretation of the data, which now suggests that the system exhibits a quantum coherence that causes a component of the superflow to interfere with its own flow, which results in a blockage of the superflow that complies with a requirement for coherent quantum interference. The data also show that a change in the drive current, the magnetic field, or the properties of the nanowires can shift this interference pattern, which may be a result of a change in the length of the nanowires. In 1999, the discovery of T-dwarf GJ 229B by Hubble Space Telescope was a significant breakthrough, however further analysis revealed that the spectrum actually belonged to L7 dwarf GJ 229, rather than the previously estimated M8 dwarf GJ 229, thanks to an inaccurate telescope calibration. A re-examination of the data using the advanced APOLLO code, renowned for its high accuracy in spectral reconstruction, is the basis for a new study. The code effectively simulates the incomplete spectroscopy by mimicking the effects of the blocked light, thereby allowing researchers to estimate the system's temperature and chemical composition. The new analysis of GJ 229B, using the code's high precision, yields a temperature of 666+6-4 K and a relatively high surface pressure of 10-100 times the standard atmospheric pressure, accompanied by cloud features, consistent with the dwarf's slow rotation period. The code also identifies an overestimated carbon content in previous analyses, suggesting the carbon absorption features actually result from CH4 and CO gases, rather than a carbon-rich composition. As a result, the code places GJ 229B in the L7-T2 dwarf spectrum range, making it the first identified T-dwarf in 1999, providing a new framework for comparing it to other T-dwarfs. Notably, the code's predictions for the system's optical and near-infrared properties are consistent with ground-based observations, and a re-examination of the data for the dwarf object 2M0437-7203 also yields similar, cloud-affected atmospheric characteristics. The study sheds new light on the composition and cloud features of this dwarf, offering a better understanding of its behavioral patterns in comparison to other T-dwarfs. Additionally, it highlights the superior retrieval capabilities of the APOLLO code, particularly in analyzing the complex atmospheric structures of these distant celestial bodies. As such, the study provides a solid foundation for a broader examination of T-dwarf characteristics using this advanced code. Furthermore, this study highlights the significance of further ground-based observations to validate the results and achieve a more precise, real-world understanding of these distant objects. The study also presents a new framework for comparing GJ 229B to other T-dwarfs in the field, using a combination of observational data and a set of cloud-affected atmospheric characteristics, and highlights the need for a thorough analysis of this dwarf's fast rotational period, supported by evidence from both the analysis of the data and the code's predictions. In this analysis, we scrutinize the interplay between thermal dissipation and strong interaction in QCD's early stage, specifically within the quark-gluon plasma. It is demonstrated that in high-energy collisions, the scattering of incoming partons off this thermal medium results in the creation of outgoing partons with significantly modified properties, exhibiting distinct spin-isospin patterns. Corresponding inelastic processes and associated scattering rates are thoroughly outlined, showcasing the fundamental role of non-perturbative forces in shaping the thermal medium's interaction with partons. A key aspect of this interplay is the significant dependence on color charge, which dictates the scattering's intricate dynamics. A crucial finding emerges in the form of an inequality, indicating that the scattering cross-section is substantially greater than expected in ideal quark-gluon plasma, thus providing a critical indicator for identifying this specific phase in heavy-ion collisions. This research is further illustrated through simulations of in-medium parton fragmentation functions, revealing distinct features that can serve as landmarks in identifying the quark-gluon plasma's properties. These results hold significant implications for further research in high-energy heavy-ion collisions, incorporating the scattering's effects within the quark-gluon plasma, in order to accurately interpret data from experiments such as the Large Hadron Collider, RHIC's BNL, and forthcoming experiments at future colliders like the LHC's CERN. In particular, this research highlights the importance of employing the full strength of strong interactions in interpreting data from heavy-ion collisions at high energies, in contrast to the assumption often used in Lattice QCD calculations. In the context of heavy-quark physics, this research shows that in heavy-ion collisions at high energies, quark-quark scattering plays a subsidiary role in comparison to quark- gluon scattering, a distinction that holds significant implications for the interpretation of data from heavy-quark experiments in heavy-ion collisions. Finally, this research demonstrates that in heavy-ion collisions at high energies, the scattering of partons off the quark-gluon plasma results in the creation of glouns out of virtual quarks, a process that, while previously considered in abstract studies of in-medium physics, has not been examined within the specific framework of parton physics. In heavy-quark physics, this research shows that in heavy-ion collisions at high energies, the scattering cross-section is significantly influenced by the creation of gluons out of virtual quarks, a phenomenon that holds significant implications for the interpretation of data from heavy-quark experiments in heavy-ion collisions. We have investigated the plasmonic properties of a specific flat-band that arises in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides.  The flat-band, located within the lattice periodicity, exhibits isolated behavior due to its lack of overlap with broader bands which would otherwise cause inter-band scattering.  Within this isolated environment, the flat-band develops unique properties that allow it to carry information in a non-local manner, akin to the phenomenon observed in superconducting rings.  We were able to demonstrate this non-local transport by showing that the response of the flat-band to an electric field is equivalent to that of an electric field applied to a specific point on the opposite side of the sample.  This unique response enables twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides to support plasmons that can propagate in a flat, two-dimensional space of independent motion.  A key characteristic of these plasmons is their uniform, uniform speed of propagation which is determined by the strength of the Coulomb interaction within the flat-band.  We were also able to show that the scattering of these plasmons off lattice defects can result in the observation of unusual, long-lived oscillations. We introduce a novel approach to regularizing neural networks by enforcing their output maps to be consistent across different input perturbations. Specifically, we propose enforcing the Lipschitz condition, which controls the magnitude of the output change in response to input variations. To facilitate computation, we transform this constraint into an enforceable constraint using the Kantorovich-Rubinstein duality, which connects the Lipschitz constraint to a constraint on the network's layer outputs. We experimentally verify the effectiveness of this approach on multiple image classification tasks, demonstrating improved performance compared to existing regularization techniques. Sequential neural network models like LSTMs are frequently applied to sequence prediction tasks but can struggle with consensus tasks due to their local information flow. We utilize the Basque verb agreement task as a benchmark to investigate this phenomenon and propose a novel method to enhance LSTM performance on such tasks by leveraging a multi-layer approach combining both strong and weak agreements. Our results demonstrate that this method yields significant improvements over standard models and even surpasses state-of-the-art solutions for the Basque task. Furthermore, we explore the theoretical aspects of sequential models in relation to consensus tasks and provide concrete insights for the Basque agreement phenomenon. Our findings are particularly relevant to English part-of-speech tagging, where our proposed multi-layer method achieves comparable performance to current state-of-the-art techniques but significantly lags in the Basque case. We conclude that the challenge of the Basque agreement task lies not in the model but rather in the task itself and suggest that our multi-layer multi-task learning framework is a viable approach for achieving strong performance on consensus tasks. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/AlvaroFontaine/basque-lstm-consensus. Our paper was initially submitted to the ICLR 2020 workshop "Machine Learning for Sequential Data" but due to editorial changes, it was not considered for publication. Now we choose to share our findings with the Natural Language Processing Community at the 2023 Findings of the Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (CVPR) track of NLP and Vision papers. Our method also achieved the second-best score on the Portuguese verb agreement task in the 2019 ICLR workshop "Machine Learning for Sequential Data". Our method is currently ranked 6th on the Basque agreement leader board with an accuracy of 92.48%. Our method consists of a multi-task learning framework that utilizes two LSTMs: a strong LSTM that is trained on rich character sequences and a weak LSTM that is trained on compact character sequences. We utilize this approach to achieve state-of-the-art performance on the Basque agreement dataset, outperforming the current leader by a margin of 0.26%. We hypothesize that the reason we are able to obtain such results is due to the fact that the Basque agreement pattern is characterized by multiple layers of agreement, a phenomenon that we confirm through a thorough statistical analysis. By utilizing scanning probe microscopy to investigate the mixed-state magnetic torque of Nd-doped Sr2CuO4, our study reveals a previously unknown phase transition in this material at very low magnetic fields. A comparison with existing theories allows us to identify this event as a transition between two vortex lattice structures, specifically between a hexagonal and a square lattice arrangement. A small change in the interlayer coupling, brought about by the doping, serves as the underlying cause for this phase change, which our findings position as an essential property common to all material systems featuring interlayer coupling that are near the decoupling transition point. Furthermore, the magnitude of the change in the critical field at the transition can be precisely controlled through the doping level, which has significant implications for utilizing the structural phase transition in Nd-doped Sr2CuO4 in the development of superconducting devices. By incorporating a new method for detecting the positional shift of vortices, our study also offers a method for enhancing the precision of measurements of the magnetic field at these structural phase transitions, which are of fundamental importance in the study of superconducting materials.

The Southern Atlantic Ridge system forms the boundary between Africa, Europe, and South America. It extends westward from 3°N to 34°S latitude and divides into two separate ridges in the South Atlantic. The southern portion of the ridge, also known as the Southern Atlantic Ridge, begins at 10°S and continues to 40°S latitude. It features a central axis with a maximum depth of approximately 4,000 meters, surrounded by deep oceanic trenches with depths ranging from 4,500 to 5,500 meters. This area is home to numerous underwater mountain ranges, with some peaks reaching within 1,000 meters of the ocean's surface. This kinematic model focuses on the Southern Atlantic Ridge between 10°S and 40°S latitude. It utilizes bathymetric data to create three-dimensional models of the seafloor and assesses the movement of the Earth's crust along this ridge system. This model identifies various features of the ridge system, including numerous underwater mountain ranges formed by non-transform discontinuities. Machine learning models working with counterfactual statements face considerable challenges due to the inherent difficulty of these statements. Counterfactuals by definition present an alternative outcome based on a different fact, which often involves modifying a sentence that describes an action's effect. This task is complicated because it entails both altering a true statement into a false one and ensuring the resulting sentence is coherent and relevant. Current methods relying on generative models or logical deductions often struggle with scale, while other approaches using supervised learning find it difficult to cover a wide range of situations. In this work, we introduce a new framework along with a specific model, called DISCO, which leverages extensive language-to-text networks to generate counterfactual statements from true descriptions. This model showcases exceptional performance on a wide range of counterfactual types, notably outperforming competitors on tasks involving phrasal counterfactuals. Our analysis of various modifications to the model reveals insights that can be applied across the counterfactual generation field, while our code's open-source nature enables seamless exploration of its capabilities. Despite achieving impressive results, we also observe limitations in our model's ability to produce highly nuanced counterfactuals from all perspectives, underscoring areas for further improvement and innovation. Our model and evaluations are now part of a publicly accessible dataset that describes counterfactuals, along with how they differ from their corresponding true statements. This dataset, though initially designed with linguistic analysis in mind, can also be useful from a human-commonsense perspective. We highlight the potential for further exploration into this dataset's social implications, especially with regards to how it defines counterfactuals and their differences. A counterfactual's scope, which refers to either a single action, a single state, or both, also presents an interesting aspect to study, while a counterfactual's polarity presents a more straightforward but essential attribute. We study counterfactuals across two primary dimensions: scope and polarity, which together present a comprehensive view of these statements. We then delve into the world of human-generated counterfactuals, compiling a large dataset from multiple crowdsourcing efforts that reveal notable differences between human-generated and model-produced counterfactuals. We explore the considerable capabilities of models like DISCO, which can accurately determine a statement's truthfulness yet struggle with grasping the underlying reasoning that this truthfulness is rooted in. This leads us to reexamine the typical counterfactual generation framework, questioning whether the direction from description to statement is always the most effective approach. We propose a new concept of global energy dissipation, which could be employed to develop more accurate numerical methods for time-fractional phase-field equations. These methods would be consistent with the physical constraints of the model, preventing unphysical energy growth. We believe our results could be extended to other time-fractional differential equations, such as the Allen-Cahn equation. Building on these findings, we are exploring new approaches to developing well-posedness proofs for time-fractional differential equations, focusing on the role of integrals in these proofs. We are also investigating additional properties of the energy function, as well as its connection to the Hodge decomposition. We are currently working on a related research paper, which focuses on the long-term behavior of the time-fractional phase-field model, including both analytical and numerical results. Quantum field theory involves using the flow of physical information for a set of observables forward to infer properties of the underlying Hilbert space, and then to derive properties of configuration spaces. This process can be represented as a bidirectional flow that is captured by an adjoint relationship, specifically a 2-categorical adjunction, which reflects the relationship between functors that map from the category of hyperfinite type III factor representations to that of compact, totally ordered spaces and then to the category of configuration spaces. The Fock space construction, which is used to map the latter category to the former, has an inverse that maps the former category back to the latter, and this inverse is represented by a natural transformation that arises from applying the Martin boundary construction. This discovery of the Martin boundary construction as the inverse of the Fock space construction provides a fundamental explanation for the similarity between the types of maps that result from the two approaches, and it enables the integration of the Martin boundary construction into the broader framework of category theory. This integrated form, which is represented as an extension of the 2-categorical adjunction to a Quillen adjunction, can be used to derive the Martin boundary construction and also to prove the uniqueness of the categorical implementation of the duality between the two categories. This uniqueness has a significant consequence for the categories of the hyperfinite type III factor representations and the compact, totally ordered spaces, which are found to be symmetric monoidal categories with an inherent property of conformal covariance. This finding further implies that the category of the hyperfinite type III factor representations is equivalent to a specific subcategory of the category of superselection representations of a chiral CFT, and this equivalence provides a basis for reconciling the mathematical approaches of Haag-Kastler and Wightman. This combined form of the Martin boundary construction, which is derived from the categorical relationship, is found to be an extension of the Wightman construction, and this extension is denoted as WKH construction. Heart conditions such as mitral valve prolapse and left ventricular hypertrophy can be difficult to diagnose using heart sound analysis due to their normal occurrence rates. This study proposes a method to analyze heart sounds with external interference and alterations in sound quality. Initially, a reference database of heart sounds under normal conditions was established and then signals with external interference and sound quality alterations were added to create test datasets. These test datasets featured various types of interference and alterations, including background noises, heart rate variations, and changes in sound quality. To differentiate between these conditions, a feature extraction method was employed, followed by a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify the heart conditions. The results of using the proposed method exceeded those of the existing state-of-the-art approach and demonstrated its potential for accurately diagnosing heart conditions from heart sounds. Furthermore, the proposed method achieved a high level of accuracy in diagnosing specific conditions, such as mitral valve prolapse, and showed no significant decline in performance when applied to unfamiliar sounds, a key challenge in heart sound analysis. The code for this research is publicly available on GitHub. This study further investigated the capacity to diagnose conditions from reduced-duration heart sounds, specifically those with a length of 0.5 seconds, and discovered that this proposed method retains its high level of accuracy. This finding is significant as it allows for the development of more efficient heart sound databases. In addition, the study demonstrated that the proposed feature extraction method is superior to existing techniques and is equally effective when applied to the classification of other medical conditions, such as snoring and stridor. This research involved a collaboration of cardiologists and audio specialists to validate the accuracy of the results and the effectiveness of the method. To ensure the reliability of the method, a secondary trial was conducted with a revised version of the database and the results of this study were verified by additional cardiologists. This study provides evidence that deep learning techniques can be highly effective at solving complex heart sound analysis problems. This research may serve as a starting point for the development of advanced heart sound analysis technologies capable of diagnosing conditions from low-quality recordings. The proliferation of wearable devices and cloud services opens up opportunities for seamless and versatile healthcare services. However, the success of cloud-based healthcare systems relies heavily on balancing user privacy with data utilization. A significant challenge in developing robust healthcare APIs is addressing the diverse health data patterns, such as sudden spikes in activity levels and heart rate data. These patterns pose difficulties for traditional machine learning algorithms when detecting anomalous health data. In response to these challenges, we present a novel approach, FedHealth, which utilizes a federated transfer learning framework to combine data from diverse sources, such as activity, ECG, and blood pressure sensors. The FedHealth framework employs a hybrid approach, leveraging both federated learning and transfer learning to adapt to new types of health data. Theoretical analyses and comprehensive experiments using activity and ECG data validate the FedHealth framework's performance, demonstrating its capacity to detect anomalous health data in collaboration with cloud services. The implementation of the FedHealth framework in a wearable healthcare app yields satisfactory results, with a 95% accuracy rate in detecting anomalous health data compared to expert-generated ground truth. The source code of the proposed framework is available online at https://github.com/hjdwng/FedHealth. The app demo is available at https://youtu.be/9T09B8IeTgA. Furthermore, the trial data is available at https://doi.org/10.20342/db-02363001. performance, but obtaining and installing these libraries is often a complex
process, hindering the effectiveness of automated testing tools. To streamline
the testing process, our approach automates the retrieval, compilation, and
linking of software libraries using a simple text-based specification, leveraging
low-level system commands and C functions to accomplish this task. To demonstrate

successfully incorporates the GNU C Library, OpenSSL, and Zlib. Our results show
that our approach converges to optimal performance, achieving a median runtime
of under 100 seconds for all tests. To facilitate ease of use and overall
efficiency, our approach should be incorporated into automated testing tools.

Time series data from life sciences typically contain information over brief timeframes, combining multiple measurement variables. Unlike statistical signal processing methods, machine learning techniques can handle these data by constructing a composite signal representation. However, when new data becomes available, learning algorithms usually need to be retrained from scratch. This research introduces an innovative approach, known as monitored learning, which allows previously trained models to assess the new data's representation accuracy and refine the model in real-time using only the new observations. We demonstrate monitored learning's effectiveness with a temporal series learning algorithm, specifically designed for data involving multiple measurement variables. When data varies significantly over time, the standard machine learning approach often performs poorly, but our monitored learning method consistently produces reliable results. Our results show that this method can accurately predict certain time series data from life sciences, such as protein expression profiles, pH levels, and electrical activity in the heart, even when the time series are short and high-dimensional. Furthermore, our method achieves this by creating a composite signal representation using a neural network, without the need for preassembling the signal representation through the decomposition of individual time series. Our code is available online at https://github.com/eperezmed/monitored-learning. This is an extended version of a previous article, which was presented at the 2019 Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Life Sciences. That article focused on predicting protein expression levels, but it did not include sufficient details on modeling raw data. This article addresses those missing details and includes additional experiments. These experiments compare our method to traditional machine learning techniques, as well as a method suggested by Rahimi and Bichot, which involves using a single linear model to model all time series data from life sciences. We tested these methods on various time series data from life sciences, such as expression levels of different genes in Arabidopsis thaliana, protein expression profiles, pH levels, and electrical activity in the heart. Our results show that our monitored learning method consistently performs better than the other methods we tested. We also discovered that, when data varies significantly over time, machine learning methods perform poorly, but this issue is resolved by our monitored learning method. Classifying musical devices, such as instruments from audio recordings, has historically been challenging due to a large number of possible categories and high data costs for manual labeling. This study introduces a novel approach, built upon a hierarchical framework, for one-shot audio classification of musical devices. We demonstrate that by recognizing relationships among devices, our method significantly improves performance, achieving exceptional results with minimal manual labeling. An agent experiences self-disapproval when it recognizes a flaw in one of its actions, and self-deprecation when it perceives a weakness in its capabilities. Incorporating self-disapproval into reward functions encourages agents to rectify mistakes made during previous experiences. In contrast, incorporating self-deprecation encourages agents to select actions that increase their perceived skill level, potentially leading to data-efficient learning. However, both self-disapproval and self-deprecation can lead to erratic behavior if not properly controlled. To mitigate this risk, a punitive mechanism is proposed that restricts an agent's behavior based on its estimated robustness. The proposed framework is applied to the problem of learning from imperfect demonstrations, and simulated experiments confirm its effectiveness in learning from a variety of datasets. Furthermore, the framework's capacity to manage the interplay between self-disapproval, self-deprecation, and punishment is illustrated through a comparison of its agent behaviors against those produced by alternative methods. The code used in these experiments is also made publicly available. Despite its e effectiveness, the proposed framework is not universally superior, as some experiments show that random controllers can, on occasion, perform as well as or better than the proposed framework. Further research is needed to fully understand the implications of self-disapproval, self-deprecation, and punitive controls in optimal policy search. The theory underlying the strongest variant of the proposed framework is also proved, providing a bound on the performance of policies optimized through the framework. This bound serves as an incentive entropy regularizer, similar to those used in entropy-regularized optimization. Moreover, a connection is established between the proposed framework and the approach of beam search, as well as the use of punitive controls to promote diversity. The potential extension of the proposed framework to other policy-based methods is also discussed, along with the challenges and potential solutions involved in incorporating self-disapproval and self-deprecation into policy gradient methods. The accuracy of visual association detectors relies heavily on the ability of models to distinguish between genuine associations and false positives that arise due to inherent flaws in data collection. The primary source of these false positives stems from the fact that only easily identifiable, central examples of a particular class are annotated during training. As a result, models excel at recognizing these classic combinations but severely underperform when presented with novel, compositional associations between visual entities. The Compositional Visual Association Detection dataset, an advancement over the standard Visual Association Detection dataset, is introduced to address this issue. This new dataset introduces more precise annotation guidelines that target a wider range of associations within each category and is employed to demonstrate the inadequacy of current visual association detectors. To overcome this limitations, a novel detection framework called Group-Fusion Visual Association Detector is proposed, featuring a hierarchical approach that amalgamates feature extraction information and employs a score-fusion strategy to broaden its capabilities to detect a variety of compositional associations between visual entities. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method achieves notable improvements to the accuracy of visual association detection, especially in detecting a variety of compositional associations between visual entities. As opposed to competing methods that primarily excel at detecting classic combinations between visual entities, our method achieves top-notch performance across the board. Our implementation code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/group-fusion-visual-association-detector. Our research findings are also featured in the paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04049. Our research team proposes the Group-Fusion Visual Association Detector method and introduces the Compositional Visual Association Detection dataset from which we have released the data at https://github.com/zwang84/Compositional-Visual-Association-Detection. Our research has been featured in CVPR'21 and the Group-Fusion Visual Association Detector method has won the 2nd place in the CVPR'21 Compositional Visual Association Detection Challenge. Our research has also been continued and we have a new paper available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01851 and we have released a new dataset called the Compositional Visual Localisation dataset at https://github.com/zwang84/Compositional-Visual-Localisation. This report outlines the development of a novel Content Addressable Parallel Processor, built with a Field Programmable Gate Array. Although content-addressable memories have been successfully implemented on FPGAs, our design uniquely integrates multiple pointers, update modes, and user-definable functions, making it an advanced, highly versatile system. Furthermore, we have successfully integrated this system with a lightweight, open-source programming framework called Pitr, which enables efficient and effective utilization of this cutting-edge hardware. A benchmark program has been developed to demonstrate the performance benefits of this technology, showcasing up to 5 times faster execution speed and significant energy savings compared to standard CPUs. Additionally, we explore the potential applications and future developments of this technology in computational science and machine learning. The fully functional hardware design, along with the modified Pitr compiler and benchmark program, have been openly contributed to the scientific community through public repositories.

Furthermore, we propose a new language design that can efficiently leverage the capabilities of this machine through the placement of specialized instructions within program loops. Comprehensive simulations have validated the performance benefits of this machine, resulting in up to 5 times faster execution speeds and substantial energy savings in various computational applications. While this solution guarantees memory safety, it introduces additional memory usage and CPU cycles. To mitigate these costs, we propose a threshold-based configuration strategy that adaptively adjusts the machine's size and memory protection strength to strike a balance between performance and memory safety in real-world applications. K2-22b, initially considered a hot Jupiter orbiting a G-type star, has undergone revisions in its planetary parameters due to observations from TESS and ground-based radial velocity data. Re-examining the dataset, we find the observed dimensions and orbit of the planet cannot be explained by its energy output, which suggests an alternative, intriguing scenario. We propose that the planet's increased energy output results from its reduced heat generated by friction within its thick atmosphere, which could amount to 79% of its current mass. This atmospheric component may also be responsible for the planet's reduced energy output in its orbit around the star. We also discover an unusual spin axis orientation of nearly 90 degrees for the star, which we believe is an indicator of angular momentum transfer from the planet to its host, likely caused by tidal interactions during their 0.48-day orbital convergence. This finding highlights the complex relationships and energy transfers within exoplanetary systems that can be uncovered through their brightness variations. Full details of our analysis are provided in a companion submission to this meeting, which includes a wealth of data on the K2-22 system (Gillson et al., \cite{gillson2021}). We hope to continue studying this system further with the anticipated results from the NEST mission, which will enable us to accurately determine the planetary parameters of K2-22b and assess the tidal heating that drives the facade of this planet. The rapid dissemination of information on social media and online platforms means false news can quickly go viral, spreading misinformation. To address this issue, detecting emergent counterfeit news is crucial. Traditional machine learning methods can struggle with such tasks due to their reliance on large, pre-labeled datasets. In contrast, our proposed framework, Meta Neural Process Networks, is well-suited for detecting emergent counterfeit news across multiple platforms by leveraging only a limited number of labeled samples from each platform. By using a mix of text, image, and category information in their respective input representations, Meta NPNs can effectively handle multiple data modalities. We evaluate our model's performance on the Facebook News Integrity Partnership Dataset, achieving superior results compared to baseline models and demonstrating its effectiveness in detecting counterfeit news on unknown platforms with limited labeled data. Notably, our approach also facilitates the discovery of false news on new platforms by only needing a small number of labeled samples from each one. We further explore the theoretical aspects of Meta NPNs in relation to existing neural network architectures, acknowledging their general applicability and highlighting the novel aspect of our method, which involves the simultaneous detection of false news utilizing multiple modalities. We publicly release the code and model parameters for this task, which can be found at https://github.com/author-name/meta-npn. To further explore these characteristics, our study introduces an infinite set of star normal quotient graphs derived from twisted wreath structures and verifies that they meet the requirements for the graph inequality, thereby proving a significant theorem. This achievement is notable because it addresses a conjecture made by Haviv, Reuter, and Zhang in 2019. This study develops a biophysical computational model of default mode network activity in the prefrontal cortex of marmoset monkeys. The model is designed to investigate the neural mechanisms underlying the default mode network's abnormal function observed in Parkinson's disease patients. The default mode network is a brain network responsible for introspective thinking, and its disruption has been linked to various psychiatric disorders. Recent marmoset Parkinson's disease models showed altered brain function associated with default mode network activity, but the underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear. To address this, we created a multi-scale computational model that incorporates detailed descriptions of marmoset brain anatomy, neuronal systems, and synapse function. The model is grounded in empirical data, including functional magnetic resonance imaging scans of marmoset brains. We simulated the marmoset default mode network and analyzed its behavior to determine the conditions necessary for robust, synchronized activity within this network. Our findings indicate that the marmoset default mode network relies heavily on a specific type of neuronal connection and that its function is sensitive to the spacing of synapses. Furthermore, our model can be used to predict the effects of Parkinson's disease on this brain network. By incorporating a wide range of empirical data, our model provides a foundation for investigating its predictions and exploring the effects of various interventions on the default mode network in marmoset monkeys with Parkinson's disease. This model can be developed further to explore the interplay between this brain network and the marmoset's behavior. Additionally, it has the potential to be applied to human Parkinson's disease research, facilitated by recent discoveries revealing that the default mode network's function in humans and marmoset monkeys shares key similarities. This research was conducted under the guidelines set by the RIKEN Center for Integrative Medical Science's animal research committee and the National Parkinson Foundation. The model's code has been made publicly available on GitHub. By integrating a wide range of empirical data, this multi-scale computational model offers a valuable resource for exploring the effects of various interventions on the marmoset's default mode network. This, in turn, can provide insights into the development of more effective treatments for Parkinson's disease. The CMS collaboration developed a prototype pixel detector to test the performance of these new sensors in conditions mimicking those of the HL-LHC. This prototype, known as the Phase-1 Prototype, incorporated eight silicon pixel modules from different developers, including the AU-OE-TT1 design, which used an 650 $\mu$m thick 3D anode layer. This report details the results of testing the prototype's reconstruction capabilities with the AU-OE-TT1 module using cosmic rays. Due to the module's large size (representing a 8x22 cm$^2$ section of the full sensor) and unusual geometry, with a 3D anode layer unlike the typical 2D design, its reconstruction proved more complicated than for standard modules. To overcome this challenge, a novel reconstruction method was developed, involving the creation of a unique cluster and set of local 3D findings for each hit. This approach enabled efficient and effective track finding across the complex geometry of the 3D module. With this method, the hit finding and 3D finding algorithms showed comparable performance to that of standard modules, demonstrating the AU-OE-TT1 module's ability to deliver accurate hit information for subsequent global track finding. This work provides valuable input for the design of future CMS pixel detectors. Furthermore, the approach developed for handling 3D sensors can also be applied to other complex geometry detectors. This research was conducted as part of a master's thesis at the University of Ottawa. The associated data was collected during a test session held in Geneva, Switzerland, at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN). Our approach demonstrates exceptional performance across multiple metrics in five diverse datasets, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods while showcasing the potential of zero-shot learning for enhancing and expanding knowledge graphs. Key features of this method include utilizing agent experiences to update policies and reduce data demands from expert demonstrations. Experimental results show that our method requires significantly fewer demonstrations than traditional methods and we provide theoretical analysis to support the method's convergence properties. We utilize 1-d fs/ps hybrid rotational coherent anti-Stokes Raman spectroscopy with dual probes to achieve pressure determination, in addition to temperature and oxygen-to-nitrogen ratio assessment. By combining time-resolved fs data with pressure information from ps probes, we can accurately determine pressure even in pressurized environments. This method shows promise for studying high-pressure reactions and obtaining precise pressure readings in concurrent O2/N2 analyses. Further optimization of our system, specifically improving nitrous oxide fs data quality, could enable the method to identify this specific gas ratio, expanding its potential applications. Our technique has been effectively utilized to analyze pressure, temperature, and O2/N2 ratios in various experiments. For instance, we used it to study the expansion of nitrous oxide gas released from a model, investigating how it interacts with its surroundings in different situations. Furthermore, we used the method to analyze the effects of varying conditions, such as pressure and oxygen presence, on reactions between hydrogen atoms and cyclopropene. Additionally, we successfully integrated the technique into a dual-spatial fs/ps Raman system, enabling the simultaneous evaluation of pressure, temperature, and gas ratios in conjunction with spatial information in our experiments. This approach has provided valuable insights into reaction dynamics, such as the extent of gas mixing in combustion and the impact of surrounding gases on reaction kinetics. Furthermore, we found that our method can be applied to studying the mechanical properties of cells by combining it with a technique that generates intense, short-duration pressures. This led to thediscovery of a critical threshold below which the mechanical properties of cells no longer affect reaction outcomes. Our method has also enabled the concurrent analysis of multiple-dimensional data in fs/ps hybrid Raman experiments, improving data utilization and paving the way for the integration of multiple optical measurement techniques with reaction cell systems. Nonetheless, our method exhibits limited sensitivity in certain situations, such as when the initial and final states of a system are similar, which can result in accurate pressure determinations being hindered by a significant systematic error. In such cases, developing a more precise method for determining pressure in conjunction with fs data, particularly in nitrous oxide-based ratio assessments, could further enhance the method's effectiveness. Despite these limitations, we believe that our method has the potential to significantly impact various fields by providing a breakthrough in the concurrent, single-shot analysis of temperature, pressure, and gas ratios in reaction cell systems. This could enable researchers to obtain a more comprehensive understanding of reaction dynamics and mechanics, as well as the effects of surrounding gases on reaction outcomes

The formation of planetary systems relies heavily on the inner workings of protoplanetary disks, which are complex systems that require three key components to interact: gas, dust, and parent stellar objects. This paper delves into the specific aspect of protoplanetary disks known as spiral density waves and whirlpools that form within them. It examines the dynamics of these structures, which can be influenced by the disk's own rotation, as well as the star's energy input and how it affects the formation of particles. It also explores the conditions necessary for whirlpools to sustain themselves, even when no external force is at play, and how this self-sustaining feature can lead to the creation of rings and gaps within these disks. This phenomenon holds significant implications for the development of planetary systems, suggesting that ring systems like Saturn's may actually be locations where gravitational instability can occur, potentially giving birth to massive planets. This idea is supported by certain observations made with the Kepler space telescope, which show a link between exoplanets and the presence of whirlpools in protoplanetary disks. Establishing a framework for further research into this area, this paper ultimately seeks to explore the relationship between whirlpools and the creation of planetary systems. It concludes with some novel predictions that can be tested with upcoming observations and a better understanding of the conditions necessary for the creation of stable whirlpools. These predictions focus on how the development of these structures is affected by the temperature of the disk, particularly in regions where particles can exist for extended periods. This temperature threshold is proposed as a key factor in identifying potential locations for planetary system creation, providing a scientific framework that can be refined with new data. This paper offers a theoretical framework that can be used to create a numerical model for predicting the formation of stable whirlpools in protoplanetary disks, a step that is outlined in a companion paper. This prediction for a specific system, known as the HL Tau disk, shows a strong match with actual observations made with the ALMA telescope, providing a powerful tool for designing future observations that can identify locations with the potential to create planetary systems. This is particularly important because it offers a more detailed understanding of the early stages of planetary system formation, a process that can lead to the creation of gravitational instability and massive planets. This difference in data distribution can pose a significant challenge to machine learning models by impeding their performance and making it difficult to train models across multiple data sets. A common approach to addressing this issue is to employ a method called minimax optimization, which involves identifying and mitigating the differences in data distributions while minimizing the variability within each data set. Doing so requires the design of efficient algorithms that can handle decentralized learning in networks. Here, we present an algorithm called Decentralized Residual Distributed Subgradient Method, DR-DSGD, capable of optimizing a sum of functions subject to a privacy constraint and handling differences in data distributions. By leveraging a new inequality and adapting an existing theory, we analyze and assess the convergence rate of our DR-DSGD algorithm, particularly in scenarios where the data sets exhibit strong variability. We also compare the DR-DSGD algorithm to existing methods, such as Decentralized Distributed Subgradient Method and Federated Averaging, and show that it yields better performance in scenarios where the data sets exhibit strong variability. Moreover, we employ our DR-DSGD algorithm to solve problems involving minimax optimization and demonstrate its effectiveness in multiple real-world applications, such as hyperparameter selection, topic modeling, and image recognition. We open-source our implementation of the DR-DSGD algorithm under the Apache License, Version 2.0, and make it available for public use. In the mid-20th century, computer scientists faced significant challenges in storing data permanently, leading to the development of innovative methods for tape and card-based input/output systems. However, these solutions failed to keep up with the explosive growth of data generated by computational experiments in physics and other sciences. In the 1960s, the rise of large-scale computing and extensive data production led to a need for high-capacity, cost-effective data storage solutions. This historical study examines the adoption of hard drives as a means of external storage in computational research, tracing the path from initial hesitations to eventual widespread acceptance. By analyzing interviews with renowned scientists and exploring various factors influencing the adoption of hard drives, this study uncovers the technological, practical, and symbolic aspects that contributed to the integration of hard drives into computational research, ultimately becoming an indispensable component of modern scientific practice. Through the lens of science studies, this study explores the complex interplay between human agents, technology, and data, highlighting the need for a more nuanced understanding of the human element in the development and utilization of computational technology. At the same time, this study offers valuable insights for today's data scientists, pointing to the significance of external storage in computational research and the need for robust data preservation strategies. In the context of the history of computing, the adoption of hard drives in computational research serves as a pivotal moment in the evolution of computational science, marking a critical juncture in which technology and methodology became inextricably linked. This study provides a valuable lesson for the current era of data-intensive science, emphasizing the importance of external storage in computational research and highlighting the need for robust data preservation strategies. Furthermore, this study offers a significant contribution to our understanding of the integration of technology and science, offering a compelling example of the complex interplay between human agents, technology, and data that is a hallmark of modern scientific practice. Using data from the VVV survey, we conducted a thorough examination of 19 previously undiscovered potential globular clusters in the Galactic bulge. Our analysis involved creating color-magnitude diagrams, estimating the reddening value, calculating the central density of potential members, and comparing the characteristics of these candidates to established globular clusters in the area. By applying these tests, we were able to provide detailed properties for the 19 potential clusters, filtering out those with insufficient data or that showed unusual characteristics. From the original list, we identified 6 promising candidates, with 4 being relatively close to the sun. Our analysis suggested that 3 of these candidates, with distances of approximately 6.5 to 10.5 kiloparsecs, had similar properties to established globular clusters in the Galactic bulge. However, the others exhibited distinct features more commonly associated with open clusters or the bulge itself. Furthermore, we established that 3 of these potential globular clusters could be found in the direction of the LMC, but were actually much farther away than the LMC itself. Our analysis also revealed a previously undiscovered dense group of 11 blue main-sequence stars with little signs of central crowding, suggesting it may be a recently formed group rather than an actual cluster, and we concluded that 5 other potential clusters required further study due to insufficient data. Our proposed protocol, called TPC, runs on a distributed architecture that enables secure, streamlined processing of point clouds, eliminating the need to transfer entire cloud datasets. Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been employed to thoroughly examine the collective states within the GDR region of $^{16}$O. By analyzing the components of the Jost function, we identify the roots that contribute to collective states and calculate the corresponding eigenenergies. Notably, we find that $^{16}$O exhibits a more complex structure than $^{12}$C, with additional roots influencing the collective states within the GDR region. The slight displacement and broadening of the collective state around 16 MeV can be attributed to an interplay between a high-lying collective state and a quasiparticle pair-breaking state. Moreover, we determine that the collective state at 22 MeV is actually a combination of a collective state at 21 MeV and a quasiparticle pair-breaking state, resulting in a decrease in its transition strength from the expected value of 10$^{-6}$. Our results support the idea that the RPA framework can be improved by incorporating the Jost function method, especially regarding the characterization of collective states within the GDR region. Furthermore, we propose that the use of the imaginary part of the Jost function can be an effective alternative to the Fock operator, potentially leading to a more precise and consistent description of nuclear collective states. Our study also highlights the importance of considering the specific structure of each nucleus when analyzing its collective states, as illustrated by the distinct characteristics of $^{16}$O and $^{12}$C within the GDR region. Lastly, we demonstrate that the method can be applied across various nuclei, paving the way for a comprehensive examination of collective states across the nuclear chart. Generating high-quality texts with a specific topic requires pinpoint precision. This task is challenging because standard language models tend to produce random outputs similar to those produced by chance models, rather than generating precise texts. We introduce a method called SparseGAN that utilizes a competing network to produce high-quality texts in a training game setup. This method involves training two networks in parallel: a main generator network that produces high-quality texts and a rival discriminator network that rejects filler texts. The Cauchy stress function theory has been the subject of interest for many decades, offering a useful alternative to direct constitutive modeling. Despite its numerous benefits, this approach has been hampered by lack of a comprehensive minimally parametrized framework. In response to this gap, we present a novel, minimally parametrized formulation that establishes a linear relationship between the displacement field and the Airy stress function. This innovative framework parametrizes the Airy stress function using only the displacement field, effectively reducing the number of unknowns by half. Building on this discovery, we derive a corresponding boundary integral equation that satisfies the biharmonic equation, thereby overcoming a significant theoretical hurdle. With this development, we explore non-trivial examples, including a cantilever beam with a notch, demonstrating that our approach produces results that align with those obtained using direct methods. Notably, our results reveal a stress intensity factor that differs by only 8% from the known value for a crack in an infinite plane, highlighting both the accuracy and limitations of this new approach. To facilitate further exploration and potential applications, we also investigate the compatibility and biharmonic equation constraints in our parametrized framework, revealing that our proposed formula inherently satisfies these constraints. As a result, we are confident that this new framework will prove useful for complex stress problems that cannot be resolved using available direct methods. Our proposal tackles two significant challenges in prompt-based task-adaptation:  understanding the task-cues and generalizing to new tasks.  To achieve this, we introduce Prompt Graphs and Prompt Embeddings to enhance the prompt-based task-adaptation method known as Prompt-based Task-adaptation via Embeddings and Schedules.  This proposed method, called HyperPrompt, uses a cue-based task-conditioning approach that utilizes Prompt Graphs and their associated embeddings to effectively process task-cues.  Through extensive experiments on diverse tasks within the GLUE benchmark, HyperPrompt demonstrates superior performance when compared to the current state-of-the-art methods.  Further, our method exhibits a notable gain in efficiency by eliminating the need for expensive learnable schedules.  Moreover, our results indicate that HyperPrompt succeeds in generalizing to new tasks with only minor adjustments to the model, thus we apply our method to adapt models for cross-domain generalization, and the improvements we achieve are substantial, with an average boost of 2.5%.  Our code is available at https://github.com/THU-OGS/HyperPrompt.  In particular, our method achieves notable breakthroughs in natural language generation and few-shot learning settings within the GLUE tasks.  With only hyperparameter tuning, HyperPrompt achieves a mathematically optimal generalization to new tasks from just a single example, which we verify through extensive few-shot learning experiments across 20 different NLP tasks.  Our method's flexibility and effectiveness in natural language generation are also clearly illustrated through experiments on the SNLI and ADITYA-CHARI Datasets.  With the success of HyperPrompt in adapting models for cross-domain generalization and few-shot learning, we expect it to become the method of choice for large-scale NLP tasks that involve model adaptation and generalization.  Our theoretical analysis of HyperPrompt can be found in the appendix at page 14, and our results on natural language generation can be found at page 15, and our results on few-shot learning can be found at page 16 of the appendix.  In the appendix at page 17, our method is compared to the state-of-the-art multi-task learning methods, and in the appendix at page 18, our method is compared to the state-of-the-art meta-learning methods.  In the appendix at page 19, our method is compared to the state-of-the-art pre-training methods, and in the appendix at page 20, our method is compared to the state-of-the-art fine-tuning methods

We examine the task of estimating a network's global parameters when its nodes and edges can be maliciously manipulated. Our focus is on small-world graphs, a class of graphs characterized by a balance between local connectivity and widespread connection. We investigate two scenarios: the first scenario involves a single malicious node with limited connections, and the second scenario involves a large number of malicious nodes. For the first scenario, we develop an algorithm that estimates a graph's diameter and average node degree with an error rate of $O(\sqrt{\log n}/n)$, where $n$ represents the number of nodes. This algorithm relies on a node's degree estimation technique, which is of independent interest as previous approaches assumed a trustworthy degree distribution. For the second scenario, we prove that no accurate estimation is possible, supported by a theorem demonstrating the unfeasibility of estimating a graph's diameter with a precision better than $O(n^{1/d})$ when a significant proportion of nodes are malicious. This finding is further substantiated by a degree detection algorithm, capable of identifying nodes with excessive connections in a small-world graph with a connectivity ratio of $\kappa$, provided that a subset of at least $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ nodes are malicious. This algorithm forms a key component of our estimator algorithm for the second scenario. Lastly, we explore a hybrid scenario, which falls between the first and second scenarios, and develop an algorithm that estimates a graph's diameter with a precision of $O(n^{1/d})$. This result indicates that in this intermediate scenario, the primary limitation is the detection of malicious nodes rather than their quantity. This discovery leads to a further examination of degree detection under enhanced conditions, including the capability to query a node's connection status to other nodes. Under these conditions, we develop an efficient estimator algorithm that yields a more precise estimate of a graph's diameter, with a precision of $O(n^{2/d})$. This algorithm employs a degree detection approach that is an extension of a previous method, utilizing multiple queries to determine a node's connections to other nodes. This detection approach is more effective than the previous method, which relied on a single query to a node's neighbors, and is a key component of our estimator algorithm. This extended degree detection approach is further capable of identifying nodes with an abnormally large number of connections in a small-world graph with a connectivity ratio of $\kappa$, provided that a subset of at least $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ nodes are malicious. These vehicles can serve as probes, providing comprehensive data about road conditions. To effectively utilize this data for quick traffic assessments, a statistical method is proposed, based on analyzing the Probes' Observed Road Conditions. For a specific road section, the method evaluates traffic conditions within a short period, considering data from multiple probes and assesses queue sizes, which is a key traffic metric. Developed for urban areas with complex intersections, the method focuses on rapid assessments, using a simple combination of traffic theory and statistical techniques. Specifically, the method utilizes the Gaussian distribution to model probes' distances from the starting point and the length of the road section, then applies inverse transformation to estimate the probability of encountering obstacles within a certain distance. To validate the method, real-world data from GPS-enabled vehicles was utilized, and results showed that it effectively identifies queues of various lengths, and even under rare conditions, the method held true in simulations. Consequently, this method represents an efficient way to analyze traffic using probe vehicles. For given parameters, all necessary calculations can be performed manually, without the need for complex software, making it an ideal approach for small-scale traffic management systems. Additionally, this method may be adapted for additional traffic assessments, such as estimating speeds and accident detection, which would significantly improve the effectiveness of traffic management systems relying on probe vehicles. A primary advantage of this method is its simplicity, minimal reliance on sophisticated software, and high efficiency in processing real-time data. A potential extension to this method could be developing a comprehensive algorithm that can handle more complex traffic conditions, such as long queues, and might also be adapted for use in freeway traffic analysis. A significant aspect of this research is the low cost of implementing and utilizing the proposed method, as it utilizes freely available statistical techniques and does not require expensive hardware or software, making it an cost-effective approach for traffic management systems. A method's performance can be subjective and may vary depending on individual perspectives, but the proposed method has shown consistent results in traffic analysis. A key benefit of this research is the provision of a comprehensive understanding of a critical traffic phenomenon, queue spread, which could be a foundation for further exploration of other critical traffic metrics, such as flow and density. Recent advances in machine learning require high-quality training data, but often encounter challenges in scaling due to the costs associated with labeling. One effective solution is to utilize multiple instructors who annotate the data simultaneously, but annotating these multiple sets of labels is expensive. To tackle this issue, we propose a Multi-Instructor Labeled Distillation framework, wherein multiple instructors provide annotations for a single dataset. To optimize the labels produced by these instructors, we employ a pairwise iterative logits coalition algorithm, which first calculates a primary distillation target based on the collective annotations, and then refines this target by selectively aggregating the labels from individual instructors. This iterative process enables the fusion of annotations under non-i.i.d. settings, and is executed using a logarithmic likelihood function that ensures a globally convergent solution. Moreover, we introduce a pair-wise soft fusion method that is resistant to outliers, and is derived from a theoretical analysis of the labels as representations of probability distributions. To accommodate a large number of instructors, we introduce an instructor filtering mechanism, which is based on the calculation of a fusion confidence for each individual instructor. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method, showing improvements of up to 6.3% in accuracy over existing distillation techniques. Additionally, our method is highly scalable, capable of handling 50-100 instructors with minimal computational overhead. Our implementation is also highly efficient, with a time complexity of O(n), making it an attractive solution for large-scale annotation settings.
