This study seeks to enhance the efficient estimation of vector bosons in high-energy muon scattering events, a process described by the weak interaction. To achieve this, we introduce a method to accurately calculate the cross-sectional area and probability of measuring the energy of the muon after the scattering event has occurred, taking into consideration the energy of the incoming muon and the energy carried away by the neutrino. By comparing our proposed method to existing estimators, we identify areas for further improvement, particularly in their limited ability to account for incoming muon energies above 10 GeV and scattering angles greater than 10 degrees. Our results demonstrate that a more precise, iterative approach to energy estimation, often referred to as the "unfolded" method, yields more accurate outcomes than the traditional, linear methods. Specifically, this study evaluates three commonly employed methods: the Strumfels iteration, the iterative 2D method, and the conventional lookup table technique. To establish a sense of reliability, our findings were cross-verified using two distinct mathematical frameworks. Furthermore, we explored additional variables, including the inherent characteristics of the detector, to further refine our understanding of this process. Ultimately, our research facilitates more precise calculations of the scattering cross-sectional area, now expressed in units of picobarns, for incoming muon energies ranging from 10 to 1000 GeV and scattering angles between 8 degrees and 179 degrees. This improved capability will enable more accurate experiments in future muon collision experiments. To illustrate the practical applications of this research, we considered the geological requirements for producing high-energy muons in the context of particle collisions involving an electron, muon, and neutrino. To further validate this research, we analyzed the characteristics of events producing a high-energy muon and observed that the estimation methods previously compared hold significance in this context as well. To make the outcomes of this study more accessible, we provide the cross-sectional area and probability estimates in a format that can be easily incorporated into detector simulation software, specifically using the established interface used by the MIMOSA software. It then selectively includes pixels from the remaining areas based on their comparison rankings and spatial location within the image. This algorithm produces a consistently high-quality sample, even in the presence of distorted images, and outperforms existing methods with a faster computation time. Our proposed method is particularly well-suited for applications involving deep neural networks, which can benefit from reduced data set sizes without a significant loss of accuracy. This article examines the relationship between the stability of a specific surface in a dynamical system and the specific surface itself. We demonstrate that in a particular class of dynamical systems, specifically those with non-local behavior as defined by Caputo derivatives, stability is automatically guaranteed for any surface that does not contain the equilibrium point. We compare this result to the one obtained for local dynamical systems, revealing that the condition of not containing the equilibrium point is necessary in the former case. Furthermore, we derive a condition for a surface to be invariant in the non-local case, and illustrate our findings through a numerical example. Finally, we consider the implications of these results for control and feedback design in the context of non-local dynamical systems. Next-generation wireless networks require exceptionally high data transfer rates that could be achieved by utilizing Terahertz frequency bands for communication. However, signal travel distance limitations in these bands force devices to communicate with each other in a multi-hop mode, using a large number of intermediate devices. Developing and fine-tuning machine learning models, particularly neural networks, rely heavily on diverse annotated datasets. Nevertheless, assembling such datasets proves challenging, mainly due to the need for multiple annotations from different experts. In the context of Arabic language processing, this difficulty is compounded by several factors including the script's reading direction, linguistics specificities, and the scarcity of resources. To streamline the annotation process for Arabic texts, we present MADARi, an integrated web platform for collaborative annotation and spelling correction. MADARi caters to multiple tasks such as text preprocessing, annotation guided by predefined criteria, and a spell checker that leverages Karpagoda's Arabic spell checking rules. To facilitate collaboration, MADARi enables multiple users to work simultaneously on different datasets, with users able to view each other's annotations in real-time. Additionally, the platform allows for the upload of raw texts and subsequently preprocessed data, including annotations and spelling corrections. All developed resources, including the spell checker and annotation tools, are made freely available for the broader research community. Furthermore, MADARi is designed with a modular architecture, enabling easy integration of additional tools and features. In line with its collaborative purpose, MADARi is an open-source platform available at https://madari.iit.edu. It incorporates a set of annotation and correction tools developed with modular architecture and flexibility in mind, and it is our hope that it will serve as a useful platform for developing machine learning models and related natural language processing tasks in Arabic. Additionally, MADARi has been successfully tested with a range of machine learning models, with results showing that even small datasets of 800-1000 instances can achieve respectable performance metrics. For instance, when evaluated on the FSDataset, a commonly used benchmark for Arabic part-of-speech tagging, it was found that a model trained with annotations from MADARi on the Fast-Standard dataset was capable of achieving an accuracy of around 92%. Planets orbiting solar-like stars experience radiation from their host stars in various spectral ranges, affecting atmospheric composition and temperature through photochemical processes. Understanding these processes is crucial for accurately interpreting exoplanet spectra and assessing habitability. This study examines how molecular abundances in the atmospheres of Earth-like exoplanets change due to stellar radiation, considering three types of stars and multiple possible planetary orbits. The research shows that atmospheres of close-orbiting planets, regardless of being dense or not, undergo significant changes, losing oxygen, methane, and water molecules. In contrast, temperate planets retain more molecules even under dense conditions, with water and methane concentrations declining slower in dense atmospheres and only when orbiting the brightest star. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have excelled in various social and infrastructure graph applications but often struggle with biomedical graph challenges due to data sparsity. Current distance-based GNNs models can lead to inaccurate results as they may propagate errors along graph paths. To resolve this issue, we introduce a new distance metric called the Lorentzian distance that considers a node's ego-features and its nearest neighbors. This distance metric forms a minimum spanning tree in a graph, thereby providing a unique path between any two nodes. We propose a novel Lorentzian GNN (LGN) model that leverages this distance metric, utilizing the minimum spanning tree structure to aggregate node representations. The LGN model significantly outperforms existing GNN models on various biomedical datasets in terms of prediction accuracy. Furthermore, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on certain benchmark tasks while being computationally efficient. We also introduce an end-to-end LGN model called Reentrant LGN (R-LGN) that matches the performance of traditional methods on certain classification tasks, while being highly efficient in terms of model parameters. A crucial aspect of our R-LGN model is its ability to attach meaningful node labels during the reentrant encoding process, thereby providing an interpretable model. Our model is open-sourced and is now available on GitHub at https://github.com/ssecaruso/Lorentzian-GNN. This work is a part of the Ph.D. thesis of the primary author, who is currently working on expanding this research in his postdoctoral studies. This paper is a revised and expanded version of our previous workshop paper presented at ICLR 2020, where it received the outstanding paper award. Our results demonstrate the LGN model's superiority over standard GNN models, while our theoretical analysis provides a rigorous background on this novel distance metric. Our experimentations are thorough, comprehensive, and report our original research findings, while our code is publicly available, enabling replication of our research findings. This study is a groundbreaking research in the field of graph neural networks, especially in the domain of bioinformatics, and our code and techniques will drive the development of innovative graph learning methods. We introduce an adjustable finite element method for solving time-harmonic diffusion problems, specifically those with smoothly varying conductivity. This approach involves a hybrid technique that combines finite element and analytical solutions. We show that our method produces an unconditionally stable numerical scheme, free from oscillations, and provide a priori error bounds for both smooth and slightly singular cases. Additionally, we demonstrate that our meshfree, adjustable approach can yield more accurate results than traditional finite element methods, even without the typical mesh refinement. We support these theoretical findings with numerical experiments in irregular domains. This method is particularly well-suited for problems with small scale variations, where traditional finite element methods can be less accurate. We also explore an alternative formulation that enables a more flexible implementation, at the cost of slightly increased computational costs. This method holds potential for solving other types of elliptic partial differential equations. We are currently investigating further developments and extensions of this method.

Using deep learning, automatic image analysis can accurately detect diseases from radiological images, such as chest X-rays, with high success rates. A notable example is the detection of COVID-19 pneumonia. However, there is a growing ethical concern about modifying medical images for purposes other than medical treatment, given that these images contain sensitive information about a person's health. In the context of chest X-rays, this issue is particularly pressing due to the high frequency of abnormal findings, which poses a continuous risk to patients' health even after initial diagnosis. This research aims to break new ground in the field by exploring methods to modify medical images in a way that takes into consideration the patient's health status. To achieve this, we developed a system that combines a health risk model and a generative model to ensure that modified images meet certain safety criteria. This system was specifically designed to handle chest X-rays and address health-related concerns. For evaluation purposes, we created a unique dataset that includes a variety of medical conditions as well as health risk factors. Our results show that our approach is effective in detecting both primary and secondary diseases from modified images, which would not be possible with conventional image-to-image translation methods. Furthermore, our empirical studies highlighted the significance of disease codes in medical imaging, a finding that we believe will be valuable to the broader research community. Our project's primary contribution is its exploration of the new concept of illness-aware image-to-image translation, which we believe has vast potential for exploration.
